south dakota.cyberbullying: S.D. Codified Laws §§ 13-32-14 to 13-32-19 — every school district must adopt a bullying policy; the definition in § 13-32-15 includes threatening use of data or computer software, and § 13-32-18 says the time or place of electronic conduct is no defense to school discipline.
south dakota.grooming: SDCL § 22-24A-5 (solicitation of a minor) — an adult 18 or older who solicits a minor (15 or younger under § 22-24A-4) by computer or other electronic means to engage in a prohibited sexual act commits a felony; consent and mistake of age are not defenses.
south dakota.overview: South Dakota handles kids' online safety mainly through schools and criminal law. Every school district must have a bullying policy that covers electronic conduct, and the state has a dedicated juvenile-sexting misdemeanor and a felony solicitation-of-a-minor law. No state social-media age-verification law was verified for South Dakota.
south dakota.report_name: South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation
south dakota.sexting: SDCL § 26-10-33 (juvenile sexting, 2012) — a minor who intentionally creates, distributes or possesses a nude or sexually explicit image of a minor by computer or digital media commits juvenile sexting, a Class 1 misdemeanor, instead of a felony under the child-pornography chapter.

tennessee.age_design: Protecting Children from Social Media Act, HB 1891 (2024), Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-18-5701 et seq. — requires social-media companies to verify account holders' ages and obtain parental consent for minors; in effect since January 1, 2025, with no injunction in place, while NetChoice's challenge (NetChoice v. Skrmetti) remains pending after a Sixth Circuit remand in August 2026.
tennessee.cyberbullying: Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-17-308(a)(5) — intentionally engaging in bullying or cyber-bullying (bullying by electronic device) is a criminal offense under the harassment law; a minor's violation is a delinquent act that can include a one-year driver's license suspension.
tennessee.grooming: Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-13-528 (solicitation of a minor) — an adult who, by oral, written or electronic communication including the internet, intentionally solicits a person they know or should know is under 18 to engage in a listed sex offense commits an offense graded one class below the offense solicited; see also § 39-13-529 (electronic solicitation).
tennessee.overview: Tennessee combines a criminal cyberbullying offense with a school-reporting duty and a new social-media age-verification law. The harassment statute makes bullying and cyber-bullying a crime, and the 2024 Protecting Children from Social Media Act requires age verification and parental consent for minors' accounts. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation runs the state's ICAC task force.
tennessee.sexting: Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-17-1003 (sexual exploitation of a minor) — knowingly possessing material showing a minor in sexual activity is a crime and applies even when the person sharing the image is also a minor; minors are handled in juvenile court.

texas.age_design: Securing Children Online through Parental Empowerment (SCOPE) Act, HB 18 (2023), Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 509 — requires age registration, parental supervision tools and limits on data collection and targeted ads for known minors; partly enjoined: a federal preliminary injunction bars enforcement of the content-monitoring and filtering duty against CCIA and NetChoice members, and the Fifth Circuit granted en banc rehearing in October 2026, vacating its July 2026 panel opinion, so litigation is ongoing.
texas.cyberbullying: Tex. Educ. Code § 37.0832 (David's Law, SB 179, 2017) — defines cyberbullying as bullying by electronic means and requires public schools to address it, including off-campus cyberbullying that interferes with a student's education or disrupts school.
texas.grooming: Tex. Penal Code § 15.032 (Child Grooming, added 2023) — a person who knowingly persuades, induces, entices or coerces a child under 18 to engage in conduct that would be a sexual offense commits a third-degree felony; see also § 33.021 (online solicitation of a minor).
texas.overview: Texas has some of the most detailed kids'-online-safety laws in this batch, including David's Law on school cyberbullying, a dedicated minor-sexting statute, a 2023 child-grooming felony, and the SCOPE Act on social-media duties for minors. Parts of the SCOPE Act are tied up in federal court, so its content-filtering duties are partly blocked while the rest remains in force.
texas.report_name: Texas Attorney General — Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC)
texas.sexting: Tex. Penal Code § 43.261 — a minor who intentionally or knowingly promotes or possesses by electronic means visual material depicting a minor in sexual conduct commits an offense graded as a misdemeanor (Class C for a first offense), with a court-ordered sexting education program under Tex. Educ. Code § 37.218.

utah.age_design: Utah Minor Protection in Social Media Act, SB 194 (2024), Utah Code §§ 13-71-101 to -401, which replaced the 2023 Social Media Regulation Act (HB 311/SB 152) — requires age assurance and default privacy protections for minor accounts; enjoined: a federal court issued a preliminary injunction in September 2024 (NetChoice v. Reyes), and the law is stayed pending a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit.
utah.cyberbullying: Utah Code §§ 53G-9-601 to 53G-9-607 — 'cyber-bullying' is defined in § 53G-9-601(5) as using the internet, a cell phone or another device to send or post text, video or an image meant to hurt, embarrass or threaten someone, and schools must prohibit it and respond to reports.
utah.grooming: Utah Code § 76-4-401 (enticing a minor) — a person who knowingly uses the internet or text messaging to solicit, seduce, lure or entice a minor (under 18) to engage in sexual activity that violates state law commits enticement of a minor, graded by the seriousness of the sexual activity solicited.
utah.overview: Utah was the first state to regulate social media for minors, but its 2024 replacement law is currently blocked by a federal court while an appeal is pending. Alongside that, Utah has school cyberbullying rules, a law against enticing minors online, and an attorney-general-run ICAC task force.
utah.report_name: Utah Attorney General — Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force
utah.sexting: Utah Code § 76-5c-205 (renumbered from § 76-10-1206 in 2025; dealing in material harmful to a minor) — the statute typically used for teen sexting; a 16- or 17-year-old faces a Class A misdemeanor and a minor under 16 a Class B misdemeanor, while adults face felony sexual-exploitation charges.

vermont.cyberbullying: 16 V.S.A. § 570 — every school board must adopt, enforce and make available harassment, hazing and bullying prevention policies at least as strict as the state model policy; 'bullying' in § 11(a)(32) includes electronic acts, including off-campus acts that substantially interfere with a student's access to education.
vermont.grooming: 13 V.S.A. § 2828 (luring a child) — knowingly soliciting, luring, manipulating or enticing a child under 16, or a person believed to be under 16, to engage in a sexual act or lewd and lascivious conduct is a crime, and it applies expressly to solicitation by electronic communication.
vermont.overview: Vermont relies on school bullying-prevention policies that expressly cover electronic acts, a juvenile sexting law that keeps first-time teen sexting in family court and off the sex-offender registry, and a luring statute that covers online solicitation. No Vermont social-media age-verification law was verified.
vermont.report_name: Vermont Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force (VT-ICAC)
vermont.sexting: 13 V.S.A. § 2802b — a minor who knowingly and voluntarily, without threat or coercion, sends an indecent picture of himself or herself by phone or computer commits a juvenile offense handled in family court, with diversion available; a first offense cannot be prosecuted as sexual exploitation of a child and does not require sex-offender registration, and the record is expunged at 18.

virginia.cyberbullying: Va. Code §§ 22.1-276.01 and 22.1-279.6 (as amended by SB 908, 2025) — 'cyberbullying' is bullying through technology, and the Board of Education's model student-conduct policies and each school board's code of conduct must address bullying and cyberbullying.
virginia.grooming: Va. Code § 18.2-374.3 — using a communications system, including computers or the internet, to solicit a child with lascivious intent is a felony (Class 5 for soliciting a child under 15, or Class 6 for procuring a minor for child-pornography offenses under subsection B).
virginia.overview: Virginia addresses online safety through school conduct codes that must cover cyberbullying, felony child-pornography laws that also apply to teen sexting, and a computer-solicitation statute for adults who target children online. No Virginia social-media age-verification law was verified in this batch.
virginia.sexting: Va. Code §§ 18.2-374.1 and 18.2-374.1:1 — Virginia prosecutes teen sexting under its child-pornography statutes: creating or distributing a sexually explicit image of a minor is a felony under § 18.2-374.1, and knowingly possessing one is a Class 6 felony under § 18.2-374.1:1, with no distinction between adults and minors.

washington.cyberbullying: RCW 28A.600.477 — every school district must adopt a policy prohibiting harassment, intimidation and bullying (HIB), defined to include intentional electronic acts, and designate a primary contact to receive complaints.
washington.grooming: RCW 9.68A.090 (communication with a minor for immoral purposes) — communicating with a minor, including by electronic communication, for immoral purposes (including grooming for sexual exploitation) is a gross misdemeanor, or a Class C felony on a repeat conviction or when done electronically; see also RCW 9A.40.090 (luring).
washington.overview: Washington requires every school district to prohibit harassment, intimidation and bullying, including electronic acts, and has a minor-specific sexting law and a law against communicating with a minor for immoral purposes. The Washington State Patrol's Missing and Exploited Children Task Force investigates online exploitation.
washington.report_name: Washington State Patrol — Missing and Exploited Children Task Force (MECTF)
washington.sexting: RCW 9.68A.053 (Sexually explicit images — crimes by minors) — Washington has a minor-specific law for teens who send or share sexually explicit images of minors, separate from the adult dealing statute RCW 9.68A.050; the legislature's 2019 Responsible Teen Communications Act also directed prevention and intervention work on teen image-sharing.

west virginia.cyberbullying: W. Va. Code §§ 18-2C-2 and 18-2C-3 — 'harassment, intimidation or bullying' expressly includes intentional electronic acts, and each county board of education must adopt a policy prohibiting it, with reporting, investigation and discipline procedures.
west virginia.grooming: W. Va. Code § 61-3C-14b — an adult over 18 who knowingly uses a computer to solicit, entice, seduce or lure a minor at least four years younger to engage in a prohibited sexual act commits a felony (2–10 years), with a harsher penalty if the adult travels to meet the minor.
west virginia.overview: West Virginia requires county school boards to prohibit harassment, intimidation or bullying, including electronic acts, and has a dedicated juvenile sexting law with an educational diversion option. Adults who solicit minors by computer face felony charges under the state's computer-crime law.
west virginia.sexting: W. Va. Code § 61-8C-3b — a minor who intentionally possesses, creates or distributes a nude or partially nude image of a minor commits an act of juvenile delinquency (not a felony), with no sex-offender registration, and W. Va. Code § 49-4-717 allows an educational diversion program before a petition is filed.

wisconsin.cyberbullying: Wis. Stat. § 118.46 — the Department of Public Instruction must develop a model school bullying policy and each public school board must adopt a policy prohibiting bullying; the model policy's definition includes bullying by electronic means, and Wis. Stat. § 947.0125 criminalizes threatening or obscene electronic messages.
wisconsin.grooming: Wis. Stat. § 948.072 (grooming of a child for sexual activity) — engaging in a course of conduct to condition, seduce, solicit, lure or entice a child for sexual contact or to produce sexual images of the child is a Class G felony, and computer or internet contact with the child is listed as a grooming act; see also § 948.075 (use of a computer to facilitate a child sex crime).
wisconsin.overview: Wisconsin requires public school boards to adopt anti-bullying policies, criminalizes threatening or obscene electronic messages, and has a specific grooming statute that lists online contact as a grooming act. Teen sexting, however, is still prosecuted under the state's child-pornography laws rather than a dedicated teen law.
wisconsin.sexting: Wis. Stat. § 948.12 — Wisconsin prosecutes teen sexting under its child-pornography law: a minor who knowingly possesses an explicit image of a person under 18 faces a Class I felony, though the 3-year mandatory minimum does not apply to offenders under 18 (Wis. Stat. § 939.617(3)).

wyoming.cyberbullying: Wyo. Stat. §§ 21-4-311 to 21-4-315 (Safe School Climate Act) — harassment, intimidation or bullying is prohibited and defined to include intentional electronic communication, and each school district must adopt a policy prohibiting it; the law covers conduct initiated, occurring or received at school.
wyoming.overview: Wyoming's Safe School Climate Act requires school districts to prohibit harassment, intimidation or bullying, including electronic communication at school, and the state has a graduated minor-sexting law that treats most teen sexting as a status offense or misdemeanor. No Wyoming online-enticement statute was verified; online enticement cases in Wyoming have been prosecuted under federal law.
wyoming.report_name: Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation — Child Sexual Exploitation / ICAC
wyoming.sexting: Wyo. Stat. § 6-4-305 (2017) — a dedicated minor-sexting law with graduated degrees: sharing your own nude image or possessing another minor's is a third-degree status offense, knowingly sharing another minor's image is a second-degree misdemeanor, and sharing or secretly capturing one to coerce, intimidate or harass is a first-degree misdemeanor; images showing explicit sexual conduct fall outside it and remain felonies under § 6-4-303.
